'''St. George''' is a neighborhood on the northeastern tip of [[Staten Island]] in [[New York City]], along the waterfront where the [[Kill Van Kull]] enters [[Upper New York Bay]]. It is the most densely developed neighborhood on Staten Island, and the location of the administrative center for the [[borough (New York City)|borough]] and for the [[wikt:coterminous|coterminous]] Richmond County. The [[St. George Terminal]], serving the [[Staten Island Ferry]] and the [[Staten Island Railway]], is also located here. St. George is bordered on the south by the neighborhood of [[Tompkinsville, Staten Island|Tompkinsville]] and on the west by the neighborhood of [[New Brighton, Staten Island|New Brighton]].

What is now St. George was initially occupied by the [[Lenape]] Native Americans, then colonized by the Dutch and the British. The first residential developments arose in the 1830s, and through the late 19th century, the area was a summer resort. Until the construction of the ferry–railroad terminal in 1886, present-day St. George was considered to be part of New Brighton. The section around the current ferry and railroad terminal was renamed after developer [[George Law (financier)|George Law]], whom [[Erastus Wiman]] promised to "canonize" in exchange for relinquishing the land rights for the terminal. Several government buildings and landmarks were constructed in St. George in the early 20th century, and further developments on the waterfront commenced in the early 21st century.<ref name="Jackson p. 1137" />

St. George is part of [[Staten Island Community Board 1|Staten Island Community District 1]].<ref name="NYCPlanning" /> St. George is patrolled by the 120th Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department]].

== History ==
=== Precolonial and colonial period ===
Originally, Staten Island was inhabited by the [[Munsee language|Munsee]]-speaking [[Lenape]] Native Americans.<ref name="NYCL p. 5">{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1994|ps=.|p=5}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|ps=.|Leng|Davis|1933|pp=71–72}}</ref><ref name="Bayles 1887">{{cite web|url=https://archive.org/details/historyofrichmon00bayl|title=History of Richmond County (Staten Island), New York from its discovery to the present time|last=Bayles|first=Richard Mather|date=1887|via=Internet Archive|access-date=November 18, 2019}}</ref>{{Rp|81–83}} The Lenape relocated during different seasons, moving toward the shore to fish during the summers, and moving inland to hunt and grow crops during the fall and winter.<ref>{{cite gotham|pages=}}</ref>{{Rp|5–23}} The present-day area of New York City was inhabited in 1624 by [[Netherlands|Dutch]] settlers as part of [[New Netherland]].<ref name="NYCL p. 5" /> In 1664, the Dutch gave New Netherland to the [[Kingdom of Great Britain|British]],<ref name="NYCL p. 5" /><ref>{{harvnb|ps=.|Leng|Davis|1933|p=107}}</ref> and six years later the British finalized a purchase agreement with the Lenape.<ref name="NYCL p. 5" /><ref>{{harvnb|ps=.|Leng|Davis|1933|p=115}}</ref>

At the time of British handover, several British, Dutch, and French settlers occupied the area, but did not have an established [[Title (property)|title]] to the land. A series of surveys were conducted through 1677, and several parcels were distributed to different landowners.<ref name="NYCL p. 5" /> Among them were the {{Convert|340|acre||abbr=|adj=on}} "Duxbury Glebe", given to Ellis Duxbury in 1708, bequeathed to the Protestant Episcopal Church of St. Andrew's ten years later,<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aPgLAAAAYAAJ&pg=PR38|title=The Earliest Volume of Staten Island Records, 1678–1813|last=Staten Island (New York, N.Y.)|publisher=The Survey|year=1942|series=Transcriptions of early town records of New York|page=38|access-date=November 18, 2019}}</ref><ref name="Proceedings of the SIAAS 1907">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9HtMAQAAMAAJ&pg=RA1-PA24|title=Proceedings of the Staten Island Association of Arts and Sciences|publisher=The Association|year=1907|page=24|access-date=November 18, 2019|issue=v. 1–2}}</ref> and then leased for 54 years by John Bard in 1765.<ref name="NYCL p. 5" /><ref name="Proceedings of the SIAAS 1907" /> Another tract was granted to Lambert Jansen Dorlant in 1680, whose western boundary was a [[Stream|brook]] on present-day Jersey Street. By 1748, it had been purchased by Salmon Comes, who ran a ferry to Manhattan. By 1765, part of the Dorlant tract was owned by John Wandel, a [[molasses]] distiller who operated a plant at the [[Kill Van Kull]] near Richmond Terrace and Westervelt Avenue, taking advantage of the Jersey Street brook.<ref name="NYCL p. 5" /> Two Native American roads intersected near the distiller: Shore Road (today's Richmond Terrace) on the [[North Shore, Staten Island|North Shore]], and a road that wound southward on St. Marks Place and then Hamilton and Westervelt Avenues.<ref name="NYCL p. 62">{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1994|ps=.|p=6}}</ref>

Fort Hill,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nypl.org/branch/staten/index2.cfm?Trg=1&d1=962&template=StGeorgeNeighborhoodHistory |title=Best of the Web |publisher=New York Public Library |date=May 19, 2014 |access-date=May 23, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1919/11/02/118175591.pdf |title=RELICS OF THE REVOLUTION – Historical Society Unearths Rich Store at Fort Hill Site on Staten Island Buttons Reveal Large Garrison. No Trace of Barracks. |date=November 2, 1919 |access-date=May 23, 2014 |work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> one of the hills overlooking the harbor, was the location on Duxbury's Point or Ducksberry Point, fortified by the British during the [[American Revolutionary War]].<ref name="Jackson p. 1137" {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080623204513/http://www.nypl.org/branch/staten/index2.cfm?Trg=1&d1=962&template=StatenIslandOldNames |date=June 23, 2008 }} Old Names on Staten Island</ref> [[Hessian (soldier)|Hessian]] troops, contracted by the British, were stationed near the Jersey Street brook,<ref name="NYCL p. 62" /> which then became known as Hessian Springs.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UwvLAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA222|title=Proceedings – Staten Island Institute of Arts and Sciences|last1=Hollick|first1=C.A.|last2=Davis|first2=W.T.|publisher=Staten Island Institute of Arts and Sciences.|year=1914|page=222|access-date=November 20, 2019|issue=v. 4–7}}</ref> After the end of the war, the area remained primarily rural through the early 19th century.<ref name="NYCL p. 62" /> The area became part of the town of [[Castleton, Staten Island|Castleton]] upon the town's Middlesex, Essex Counties, New Jersey: Environmental Impact Statement|page=433|access-date=November 20, 2019}}</ref><ref name="Stephen 2004">{{Cite journal|last=Stephenson|first=Kathryn|date=January 1, 2004|title=The Quarantine War: the Burning of the New York Marine Hospital in 1858|journal=Public Health Reports|volume=119|issue=1|pages=79–92|doi=10.1177/003335490411900114|pmid=15147652|pmc=1502261}}</ref> The state then gave {{Convert|5|acre||abbr=}} to the [[Federal government of the United States|federal government]] for the [[St. George Coast Guard Station|U.S. Light-House Depot Complex]], a [[lighthouse]] facility.<ref name="NYCL p. 62" />

=== 19th century ===

==== Early ownership ====
[[File:The Million Dollar Retaining Wall, St. George, Staten Island, N.Y. (road wall at edge of train yard by ferry slips) (NYPL b15279351-104695).tiff|thumb|"The Million Dollar Retaining Wall, St. George, Staten Island"|alt=|left]]Among the first people to promote the widespread development of Staten Island was former U.S. vice president [[Daniel D. Tompkins]], who purchased land in the northern part of Staten Island in the early 1810s. Tompkins purchased Abraham Crocheron's farm, located on present-day Jersey Street south of Richmond Terrace, in 1814. The next year, he acquired {{Convert|700|acre||abbr=}} from St. Andrew's Church, and two years after that, he bought Philip Van Buskirk's land claim, located between the two disconnected pieces of land.<ref>{{harvnb|ps=.|Leng|Davis|1933|pp=221–228}}</ref><ref name="NYCL p. 62" /> Tompkins also incorporated the Richmond Turnpike Company to build present-day [[Victory Boulevard (Staten Island)|Victory Boulevard]] in 1816, started operating a ferry to Manhattan in 1817, and laid out the adjacent village of [[Tompkinsville, Staten Island|Tompkinsville]] for development between 1819 and 1821.<ref name="NYCL p. 62" /><ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.silive.com/northshore/index.ssf/2014/11/12_things_to_know_about_histor.html|title=13 things to know about Tompkinsville, where European settlers arrived 375 years ago|last=Sherry|first=Virginia N.|date=November 30, 2014|work=[[Staten Island Advance]]|access-date=September 19, 2017|language=en-US}}</ref> Tompkins then expanded the Van Buskirks' old farmhouse, using it as his primary residence.<ref name="Jackson p. 1137" /> He died in 1825.<ref name="NYCL p. 62" /><ref>{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/ourvicepresident00dunl|url-access=registration|title=Our vice-presidents and second ladies|last=Dunlap|first=Leslie|publisher=Scarecrow Press|year=1988|isbn=978-0-8108-2114-9|location=Metuchen, N.J|pages=[https://archive.org/details/ourvicepresident00dunl/page/32 32]–34|oclc=17650377}}</ref>

Tompkins's property within present-day St. George was sold in April 1834 to Manhattan developer [[Thomas E. Davis]], who continued to buy land through the following year.<ref>{{harvnb|ps=.|Leng|Davis|1933|pp=226–227}}</ref><ref name="NYCL p. 7">{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1994|ps=.|p=7}}</ref> Davis came to own all the land on Staten Island's northeastern shore, bounded to the south by Victory Boulevard, to the west by [[Sailors' Snug Harbor]], and to the north and east by the waterfront. He planned to develop the area into a summer retreat called [[New Brighton, Staten Island|New Brighton]], renaming Shore Road to Richmond Terrace, and the first five [[Greek Revival architecture|Greek Revival]] summer bungalows were erected in 1835. Davis sold the development to a five-person syndicate for $600,000 in 1836, and the New Brighton Association was incorporated that April. The area on the northeast shore, including present-day St. George, thus came to be called New Brighton.<ref name="NYCL p. 7" /><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/008728916|title=Articles, &c. of the New Brighton Association.|last=New Brighton Association.|date=1836|location=N.Y.}}</ref>

==== Increasing development ====
Development on the New Brighton street grid proceeded according to a plan that surveyor James Lyons had created in 1835. Streets were arranged around existing topography.<ref name="NYCL p. 62" /> When the New Brighton Association laid out streets in northeastern Staten Island, many of these roads were named after notable politicians, with such names as Hamilton Avenue, Jay Street, and Madison Street. Other streets were named after people or places that were associated with the development of the area, including Tompkins, Davis, or the [[Stuyvesant family]] (who were early investors). For instance, St. Marks Place was named after Davis's developments on [[St. Marks Place (Manhattan)|St. Marks Place]] in Manhattan, while Westervelt Avenue was named after Tompkins's son-in-law.<ref name="NYCL p. 7" /> Several of these street names replaced preexisting appellations.<ref>{{Cite book|url=http://archive.org/details/statenislandname00davi|title=Staten Island names ; ye olde names and nicknames|last1=Davis|first1=William Thompson|last2=Leng|first2=Charles William|last3=Staten Island Institute of Arts and Sciences. cn|date=1896|publisher=New Brighton, N.Y., Natural Science Association|others=Allen County Public Library Genealogy Center}}</ref>

[[File:St Peters RC Ch SI jeh.JPG|right|thumb|[[St. Peter's Church (Staten Island)|St. Peter's Church]]]]

Work on the street grid and development of the land continued, but in March 1837, one major investor declared bankruptcy following the [[Panic of 1837]].<ref name="NYCL p. 7" /> The same year, the Pavilion Hotel opened in a mansion along the shore, being converted from a residence.<ref>{{citation|title=Pavilion, New Brighton|date=July 15, 1837|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2y4ZAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA527|work=The Plain Dealer|location=NY|oclc=11777382}}</ref><ref name="Leng Davis p. 230">{{harvnb|Leng|Davis|1933|ps=.|p=230}}</ref> The association continued to lay out streets. However, in 1840, four of the five original New Brighton Association investors' properties were [[Foreclosure|foreclosed upon]].<ref name="NYCL p. 7" /> The foreclosed lots were thus repurchased by Thomas E. Davis in 1844. According to a survey conducted the following year, several streets had been laid out in modern-day St. George, including Carroll Place, Hamilton Avenue, St. Marks Place, Richmond Terrace, and numerous smaller streets. Most development was on the waterfront, where there were mansions with carriage buildings, as well as smaller homes and the Pavilion Hotel.<ref name="NYCL p. 9">{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1994|ps=.|p=9}}</ref> [[St. Peter's Church (Staten Island, New York)|St. Peter's Church]] on Carroll Street was dedicated in 1844 as the island's first [[Catholic Church|Roman Catholic]] house of worship.<ref name="NYCL p. 9" /><ref name="C. 2017">{{cite web|url=https://www.silive.com/news/2017/06/father-son_team_volunteering_t.html|title=After 30 years, bells to ring again at historic Staten Island church|last=C.|first=Diane|date=June 19, 2017|website=silive|access-date=November 22, 2019}}</ref>

By the 1840s and 1850s, New Brighton began to develop into a summer resort area.<ref>{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1994|ps=.|p=10}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|ps=.|Leng|Davis|1933|pp=249–251}}</ref> In addition to the existing Pavilion,<ref name="Leng Davis p. 230" /> hotels in modern-day New Brighton included the Peteler (later St. Marks) Hotel,<ref>{{harvnb|Leng|Davis|1933|ps=.|p=938}}</ref> as well as the Belmont Hotel.<ref name="NYCL p. 11">{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1994|ps=.|p=11}}</ref> Additionally, new houses such as [[Italianate architecture|Italianate]] villas were built, while existing Richmond Terrace mansions were expanded or received new annexes and gardens.<ref name="NYCL p. 11" /> Several greenhouses were also built in the neighborhood, particularly on the land of the merchant John C. Green, part of whose estate is now the site of [[Curtis High School]].<ref name="NYCL p. 11" /><ref>{{harvnb|Leng|Davis|1933|ps=.|p=902}}</ref> The silk printer John Crabtree established a printing plant for his company, [[Crabtree and Wilkinson]], on the eastern bank of the Jersey Street brook in 1844.<ref name="NYCL p. 11" /><ref name="Lundrigan 2004">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-p4lHNbJfE8C&pg=PA43|title=Staten Island: Isle of the Bay|last=Lundrigan|first=M.|publisher=Arcadia|year=2004|isbn=978-0-7385-2443-6|series=Making of America series|pages=43–44|access-date=November 22, 2019}}</ref>{{Rp|43–44}} The factory had over 180 workers and a small residential and commercial community by 1853, and the establishment of similar factories led to the population of New Brighton doubling between 1840 and 1860.<ref name="NYCL p. 11" />

In 1858, angry Staten Island residents burned down the Quarantine in what became known as the [[Staten Island Quarantine War]].<ref name="NYCL p. 62" /><ref name="Stephen 2004" /><ref name="Cross Harbor Freight Movement Project" /><ref>{{harvnb|Leng|Davis|1933|ps=.|pp=265–266}}</ref> Three years afterward, the onset of the [[American Civil War]] resulted in large changes to the neighborhood's land use. Initially, the local economy suffered due to cessation of trade with the [[Southern United States]], but because of the [[Union Army]]'s demand for material, many entrepreneurs and workers moved to New York City, including to Staten Island's North Shore. According to a 1865 article from the ''Richmond County Gazette'', "the demand for dwelling houses upon the island has never before been equalled."<ref name="NYCL p. 12">{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1994|ps=.|p=12}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.silive.com/homegarden/interiordesign/2011/03/real_estate_boom_circa_1863.html|title=Real estate boom, circa 1863|last=Ferreri|first=James G.|date=March 25, 2011|website=silive|access-date=November 22, 2019}}</ref> During this time, many new houses were designed in the [[Napoleon III style|Second Empire style]] and/or as [[Duplex (building)|duplexes]], particularly on as-yet-undeveloped plots along Westervelt Avenue or St. Marks Place.<ref name="NYCL p. 12" /> The end of the Civil War, cheaper building materials, and technological improvements resulted in an increase in real estate prices on the North Shore, and by the early 1870s, the area was described as being prosperous, with real estate in high demand.<ref name="NYCL pp. 13-14">{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1994|ps=.|pp=13–14}}</ref>

The [[Panic of 1873]] resulted in a near-cessation of building activity on the North Shore. By the late 1870s, industries had started to move to the area again, such as J. B. King and Company, whose plaster mill opened in 1877.<ref name="NYCL pp. 13-14" /> A water system was established upon the Staten Island Water Supply Company's 1879 incorporation,<ref name="Lundrigan 2004" />{{Rp|153}}<ref name="NYCL pp. 13-14" /> and a sewage system was added between 1884 and 1890.<ref name="NYCL pp. 13-14" />

==== Renaming and late 19th century ====
In the 1880s, the area closest to the ferry terminals on the northeastern shore became known as "St. George", after developer George Law, who acquired rights to the New Brighton waterfront at bargain prices. According to island historians [[Charles W. Leng|Charles Leng]] and [[William T. Davis]], the businessman [[Erastus Wiman]], who was expanding the [[Staten Island Railway]] to New Brighton, promised to "canonize" Law if the latter agreed to relinquish the land rights for a new railroad–ferry terminal there.<ref name="Jackson p. 1137" /><ref name="Leng Davis p. 349">{{harvnb|ps=.|Leng|Davis|1933|p=349}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1929/05/26/91798618.pdf|title=Staten Island Ferry Terminal Named to 'Canonize' George Law|date=May 26, 1929|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=October 8, 2015}}</ref><ref name="NYCL p. 15">{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1994|ps=.|p=15}}</ref> St. George was selected for the terminal due to the site being the closest point from Staten Island to Manhattan, approximately a {{convert|5|mi|km|abbr=|adj=on}} distance.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qfZ0VxuLoc0C&pg=PA416|title=The Wheels That Drove New York: A History of the New York City Transit System|author1=Roger P. Roess|author2=Gene Sansone|date=August 23, 2012|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-3-642-30484-2|pages=416–}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://thethirdrail.net/0201/sirt1.html|title=State Island Rapid Transit: The Essential History|last1=Leigh|first1=Irvin|last2=Matus|first2=Paul|date=January 2002|website=thethirdrail.net|publisher=The Third Rail Online|access-date=June 27, 2015}}</ref> The [[St. George Terminal]] opened in early 1886.<ref name="NYCL p. 15" /><ref>{{cite news|url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1886/01/17/103950064.pdf|title=Rapid Transit on Staten Island|date=January 17, 1886|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=July 24, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.silive.com/specialreports/index.ssf/2011/03/for_erastus_wiman_st_george_wa.html|title=For Erastus Wiman, St. George was a golden opportunity|author1=Staten Island Advance|date=March 27, 2011|website=[[SILive.com]]|publisher=[[Staten Island Advance]]|location=[[Staten Island]], [[New York (state)|New York]]|access-date=October 8, 2015|author1-link=Staten Island Advance}}</ref> It was served by a [[Staten Island Ferry]] route to Manhattan's [[Whitehall Terminal]], as well as three routes of the Staten Island Railway: the [[North Shore Branch]] to [[Elm Park station (Staten Island Railway)|Elm Park station]] (later to [[New Jersey]]), the East Shore Branch to [[Tottenville station]], and the [[South Beach Branch]] to [[South Beach station]].<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1xFtQGUUaxYC&q=staten+island+railway&pg=PA37|title=Royal Blue Line: The Classic B&O Train Between Washington and New York|last1=Harwood|first1=Herbert H.|date=2002|publisher=JHU Press|isbn=978-0-8018-7061-3|access-date=November 17, 2015}}</ref>{{Rp|37}}

With the completion of the Staten Island Railway, Wiman's [[Staten Island Amusement Company]] started operating locations in both St. George and [[Mariners Harbor, Staten Island|Erastina]] (now Mariners Harbor).<ref name="NYCL p. 15" /> The St. George location opened in 1886 and included an illuminated fountain,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1886/07/16/archives/caught-from-a-rainbow-crowds-delighted-with-the-illuminated.html|title=Caught from a Rainbow.; Crowds Delighted with the Illuminated Fountain at St. George.|date=July 16, 1886|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|access-date=November 24, 2019}}</ref> as well as public events and competitions, a 60-piece military band, and the [[St. George Cricket Grounds]].<ref name="Jackson p. 1137" /><ref name="NYCL p. 15" /><ref name="Leng Davis pp. 318-319">{{harvnb|ps=.|Leng|Davis|1933|pp=318–319}}</ref> The fountain was removed from the site by 1887,<ref name="Leng Davis pp. 318-319" /> and the amusements in St. George ceased to exist by 1889.<ref name="NYCL p. 15" /> The grandest and last hotel of St. George and New Brighton was the Hotel Castleton, built in 1889 and destroyed by fire in 1907.<ref name="Sherry 2016">{{Cite web|url=https://www.silive.com/entertainment/2016/01/old_st_george_a_walking_tour_b.html|title='Old' St. George: Take this tour back into history|last=N|first=Virginia|date=January 31, 2016|website=silive|language=en|access-date=November 23, 2019}}</ref>

The completion of new transportation options also resulted in further real estate development, especially around the areas close to [[New Brighton station (Staten Island Railway)|New Brighton]] and St. George stations. Developers such as [[John M. Pendleton]] and [[Anson Phelps Stokes]] constructed cottages and houses in the northern part of St. George, while existing property owners expanded their properties. Many newer houses, meanwhile, were designed in the [[Queen Anne style architecture|Queen Anne]], [[Shingle style architecture|Shingle]], and [[Colonial Revival architecture|Colonial Revival]] styles.<ref>{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1994|ps=.|pp=16–17}}</ref> In 1898, Staten Island was consolidated with New York City, and this move accelerated development of the region. At this time immigrant groups settled in New Brighton in greater numbers; Italians and African-Americans along the Kill Van Kull, and Jewish communities on the eastern boundary of the village near St. George and Tompkinsville.<ref name="Jackson p. 1114">{{harvnb|ps=.|Jackson|2010|p=1114}}</ref> [[George Cromwell]], the first Staten Island borough president following the unification of New York City, decided to move the Richmond county capital from [[Richmondtown, Staten Island|Richmondtown]] to St. George, citing its convenience to Manhattan.<ref name="NYCL p. 18">{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1994|ps=.|p=18}}</ref><ref name="Leng Davis pp. 355-356">{{harvnb|Leng|Davis|1933|ps=.|pp=355–356}}</ref>

In the years after unification, the North Shore became quickly urbanized, and the political and economic center of Staten Island shifted to the region.<ref name="Jackson p. 1114" /> Development of St. George turned mostly to residential and commercial uses by the 1900s.<ref name="Waite 1987">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/07/19/realestate/if-you-re-thinking-of-living-in-st-george.html|title=If You're Thinking of Living in; St. George|last=Waite|first=Thomas L.|date=July 19, 1987|work=The New York Times|access-date=November 22, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Several government buildings were also built in the area because of Cromwell's decision to make St. George the primary civic center for Staten Island.<ref name="NYCL p. 18" /><ref name="Leng Davis pp. 355-356" /> The area's first secondary school, [[Curtis High School]], opened in 1904.<ref>{{harvnb|ps=.|Jackson|2010|p=338}}</ref><ref name="Leng Davis pp. 355-356" /><ref name="EDC p. 4">{{harvnb|ps=.|Economic Development Corporation|2009|p=4 (PDF p. 5)}}</ref> The ferry service to Whitehall Terminal was transferred to municipal operation the following year.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1905/10/26/101369958.pdf|title=TWENTY-MINUTE FERRY TO STATEN ISLAND NOW; Mayor Said: "Go Ahead, Bunt," and the First Boat Was Off. JOYFUL DAY IN RICHMOND McClellan, Cromwell, and Others Speak -- Schedule Knocked Out Last Night by the Nasty Weather.|date=October 26, 1905|work=The New York Times|access-date=November 17, 2017|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Subsequently, St. George became more urbanized due to easy access to the ferry, and because of its consolidation with New York City. By 1912, electric streetlights were being installed, and various commercial and government buildings were being erected in St. George.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1912/10/13/archives/staten-island-presents-object-lesson-of-wise-and-practical-city.html|title=STATEN ISLAND PRESENTS OBJECT LESSON OF WISE AND PRACTICAL CITY PLANNING; Noteworthy Civic Centre for Richmond Borough Opposite Ferry Approach at St. George -- Necessary Public Improvements Laying Foundation for Future Growth -- Increasing Demand for Small Houses Apparent This Season -- Two-Family Homes and Apartments Becoming More Popular.|date=October 13, 1912|work=The New York Times|access-date=November 24, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Other city services were also brought to Staten Island following unification, such as schools, emergency facilities, new roads, and utilities including an underground water supply.<ref name="NYCL p. 19">{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1994|ps=.|p=19}}</ref>

The [[architecture|architectural]] firm of [[Carrère and Hastings]] developed several buildings in St. George, including the [[St. George Library Center]] of the [[New York Public Library]] (1907), the present [[Staten Island Borough Hall]] (1906), and the [[Richmond County Courthouse (Staten Island)|Richmond County Courthouse]] (1919).<ref name="NYCL p. 18" /><ref name="EDC pp. 4-6">{{harvnb|ps=.|Economic Development Corporation|2009|pp=4–6 (PDF pp. 5, 8, 12)}}</ref> The [[Staten Island Museum]] moved to its present location in the neighborhood in 1918.<ref name="EDC p. 6" /> The 120th Police Precinct building on Richmond Terrace was finished in 1923,<ref name="EDC pp. 4-6" /><ref name="NYCL-2058">{{cite web|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/2058.pdf|title=120th Police Precinct Station House|date=June 27, 2000|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=November 16, 2019}}</ref> resulting in the consolidation of three former [[New York City Police Department]] precincts on the North Shore.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1923/11/09/archives/new-police-station-on-states-island-enright-consolidates-three-old.html|title=NEW POLICE STATION ON STATES ISLAND; Enright Consolidates Three Old Precincts in Opening Quar- ters at St. George.|date=November 9, 1923|work=The New York Times|access-date=November 24, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Other notable buildings developed in St. George during the 1920s and 1930s include the [[St. George Theatre]] (1927), the Staten Island Federal Office Building (1931), the [[Richmond County Family Court]] (1931), and the Staten Island Savings Bank (1936).<ref name="EDC pp. 4-6" /> Development of buildings in St. George increased following [[World War I]], with one person stating that Stuyvesant Place "look[ed] like a ravine" due to the pace of new residential construction.<ref name="NYCL p. 19" /> ''The New York Herald'' said in 1919 that "In St. George are excellent public and private schools as well as churches, stores and modern apartment buddings."<ref name="NYH-Charms-1919" />

The [[Staten Island Tunnel]], a railroad/[[rapid transit]] tunnel to Brooklyn, was proposed in 1912 in conjunction with the [[Dual Contracts]] of the [[New York City Subway]].<ref name="Sherry 2016" /><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1919/02/13/archives/to-act-this-year-on-richmond-tube-route-approved-in-1912-still.html|title=To Act This Year on the Richmond Tube: Route Approved in 1912 Still Alive-May Soon Be Adopted Anew or Amended|date=February 13, 1919|work=The New York Times|access-date=November 24, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> It was hoped that the completion of the tunnel would spur the development of inner Staten Island and St. George, as a trip to Manhattan via the tunnel was expected to take only 12 to 15 minutes, compared to 25 on the ferry.<ref name="NYH-Charms-1919">{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/41529904/|title=Staten Island, Least Known and Most Unexploited Section of Greater New York, Has Numerous Charms|work=New York Herald|date=May 4, 1919|access-date=January 2, 2020|via=newspapers.com|page=25}}</ref> However, after several delays and a groundbreaking in 1923, the project was canceled in 1925.<ref name="Sherry 2016" /><ref>{{cite book|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=A51VbeqTwogC&pg=PT177|title=Six Bridges: The Legacy of Othmar H. ==== Later 20th century ====
As early as 1919, "St. George" was used to describe the northeastern waterfront of Staten island as well as the hills immediately adjacent to the ferry terminal.<ref name="NYH-Charms-1919" /> By the 1930s, the "St. George" name had come to generally describe the northeastern corner of Staten Island, including what was formerly known as New Brighton.<ref name="Leng Davis p. 349" /><ref name="NYCL p. 19" /> Around this time, many of the older housing stock in St. George were converted to small apartment buildings.<ref name="NYCL p. 20">{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|1994|ps=.|p=20}}</ref> The U.S. Light-House Depot Complex was turned over to the [[United States Coast Guard]] in 1936.<ref name="Jackson p. 1137" /> After a fire burned down the St. George Terminal in 1946, a rebuilt terminal opened in 1951 with a parking lot, new ferry slips, and improved connections to buses and the railroad.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1951/06/08/archives/new-ferry-depot-will-open-today-21000000-ferry-terminal-to-be.html|title=New Ferry Depot Will 'Open' Today; $21,000,000 Ferry Terminal to Be Dedicated Today|date=June 8, 1951|work=The New York Times|access-date=November 24, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

By the 1960s, office space was being developed around Bay Street.<ref name="Waite 1987" /> The opening of the [[Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge]] in 1964 created a connection between Staten Island and the rest of New York City that did not require passing through St. George, and led to the development of neighborhoods further inland.<ref name="Jackson p. 1137">{{harvnb|ps=.|Jackson|2010|p=1137}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/11/21/archives/staten-island-pushed-into-a-new-era.html|title=Staten Island Pushed Into a New Era|date=November 21, 1964|work=The New York Times|access-date=November 24, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Furthermore, the Coast Guard complex closed in 1965, its operations being moved to [[Governors Island]].<ref name="EDC p. 6" />  By the 1970s, there was a decline in demand for St. George's residential stock.<ref name="Waite 1987" /> Only one project was completed on the North Shore waterfront in that decade, a 440-unit apartment building near the ferry terminal. Developer [[William Zeckendorf]] and materials company [[Alcoa]] had jointly proposed a 27-story residential complex on the waterfront about {{Convert|600|ft||abbr=}} south of the terminal, replacing ten industrial buildings formerly used by the American Dock Company. However, the site remained unused until 1981, when construction started on a smaller development called the Bay Street Landing.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/05/24/realestate/waterfront-in-st-george-getting-loft-apartments.html|title=Waterfront in St. George Getting Loft Apartments|last=Goodman|first=George W Jr.|date=May 24, 1981|work=The New York Times|access-date=November 24, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Further inland, St. George was mostly composed of single-family housing situated amid the area's steep topography and winding roads. Several parcels, such as the former Daniel Low Terrace, lay undeveloped.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/07/14/realestate/staten-island-s-shore-primed-for-growth.html|title=Staten Island's Shore Primed for Growth|last=Johnson|first=Kirk|date=1985-07-14|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-12-01|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

== Demographics ==

For census purposes, the New York City Department of City Planning classifies St. George as part of a larger Neighborhood Tabulation Area called St. George-New Brighton SI0101. This designated neighborhood had 20,549 inhabitants based on data from the [[2020 United States census|2020 United States Census]]. This was an increase of 1,775 persons (9.5%) from the 18,774 counted in [[2010 United States census|2010]]. The neighborhood had a population density of 33.0 inhabitants per acre (14,500/sq mi; 5,600/km<sup>2</sup>).<ref name="New York City Department of Planning 2020">{{Cite web|url=https://popfactfinder.planning.nyc.gov/explorer/ntas/SI0101|title=Census Data for SI0101|date=2020|access-date=November 27, 2025|website=New York City Department of Planning}}</ref>

The racial makeup of the neighborhood was 21.4% (4,394) [[White Non-Hispanic|White (Non-Hispanic)]], 31.9% (6,561) [[Black Non-Hispanic|Black (Non-Hispanic)]], 7.2% (1,471) [[Asian (U.S. Census)|Asian]], and 5.3% (1,074) from two or more races. [[Hispanic (U.S. Census)|Hispanic]] or [[Latino (U.S. Census)|Latino]] of any race were 34.3% (7,049) of the population.<ref name="New York City Department of Planning 2020" />

According to the [[2020 United States census|2020 United States Census]], this area has many cultural communities of over 1,000 inhabitants. This include residents who identify as [[Mexican Americans|Mexican]], [[Stateside Puerto Ricans|Puerto Rican]], [[Irish Americans|Irish]], [[Italian Americans|Italian]], and [[African Americans|African-American]].<ref name="New York City Department of Planning 2020" />

The largest age group was people 25-39 years old, which made up 22% of the residents. 59.6% of the households had at least one family present. Out of the 7,732 households, 27.8% had a married couple (10.8% with a child under 18), 6.6% had a cohabiting couple (2.3% with a child under 18), 24.7% had a single male (2% with a child under 18), and 40.9% had a single female (11.3% with a child under 18). 31.1% of households had children under 18. In this neighborhood, 70.2% of non-vacant housing units are renter-occupied.<ref name="New York City Department of Planning 2020" />

The entirety of Community District 1, which comprises St. George and other neighborhoods on the North Shore, had 181,484 inhabitants as of [[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene|NYC Health]]'s 2018 Community Health Profile, with an average life expectancy of 79.0 years.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{RP|pp=2, 20}} This is lower than the median life expectancy of 81.2 for all New York City neighborhoods.<ref name="nyc.gov 2016"/>{{Rp|53 (PDF p. 84)}}<ref>{{cite web |title=New Yorkers are living longer, happier and healthier lives|website=New York Post|last=Short|first=Aaron|date=June 4, 2017|url=https://nypost.com/2017/06/04/new-yorkers-are-living-longer-happier-and-healthier-lives/|access-date=March 1, 2019}}</ref> Most inhabitants are youth and middle-aged adults: 24% are between the ages of between 0–17, 27% between 25 and 44, and 26% between 45 and 64. The ratio of college-aged and elderly residents was lower, at 10% and 13% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{RP|p=2}}

As of 2017, the median [[household income]] in Community District 1 was $48,018.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://censusreporter.org/profiles/79500US3603903-nyc-staten-island-community-district-1-port-richmond-stapleton-mariners-harbor-puma-ny/|title=NYC-Staten Island Community District 1--Port Richmond, Stapleton & Mariner's Harbor PUMA, NY|access-date=July 17, 2018}}</ref>  In 2018, an estimated 21% of St. George and the North Shore residents lived in poverty, compared to 17% in all of Staten Island and 20% in all of New York City. One in fourteen residents (7%) were unemployed, compared to 6% in Staten Island and 9% in New York City. Rent burden, or the percentage of residents who have difficulty paying their rent, is 51% in St. George and the North Shore, compared to the boroughwide and citywide rates of 49% and 51% respectively. Based on this calculation, {{as of|2018|lc=y}}, St. George and the North Shore are considered high-income relative to the rest of the city and not [[Gentrification|gentrifying]].<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{RP|p=7}}

=== Religious structures ===
The [[Brighton Heights Reformed Church]], located at 320 St. Marks Place, was protected as a NRHP site and as a city landmark in 1982 and 1967, respectively.<ref name="nris" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.neighborhoodpreservationcenter.org/db/bb_files/1967-BrightonHeightsReformedChurch.pdf|title=The Brighton Heights Reformed Church|date=October 12, 1967|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=November 22, 2019}}</ref> The original church burned down in an accidental fire in 1996 and was rebuilt in 1999.<ref name="NYT-StG-1999" /><ref name="AIA5 p. 899">{{harvnb|White|Willensky|Leadon|2010|ps=.|p=899}}</ref> [[St. Peter's Church (Staten Island, New York)|St. Peter's Church]] on Carroll Street, dedicated in 1844, was the island's first [[Catholic Church|Roman Catholic]] house of worship. === Houses ===
The Fort Hill area comprises the remains of the streets and homes where the descendants of the Tompkins, Westervelt, and Low families lived. The area included the mansions of Daniel D. Tompkins, Anson Phelps-Stokes, and Daniel Low. Another prominent landowner was [[August Belmont]], whose name is enshrined in Belmont Place. Many of the houses remaining today represent the homes and summer homes of the Low-Tompkins extended family and friends. The residential Fort Hill area includes many examples of [[Victorian architecture|Victorian]], [[Tudor architecture|Tudor]], [[Shingle style architecture|Shingle style]], and [[Art Deco]] architecture, in addition to one house modeled after a Spanish castle.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/09/18/realestate/18hunt.html|title=Looking For a House And a Turret|date=September 18, 2005|work=The New York Times|access-date=April 25, 2016|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.timeout.com/newyork/articles/house-home/1842/house-call|title=House call: Animal kingdom|date=April 4, 2007|magazine=Time Out New York|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071211135113/http://www.timeout.com/newyork/articles/house-home/1842/house-call|archive-date=December 11, 2007}}</ref><ref name="AIA5 p. 900">{{harvnb|White|Willensky|Leadon|2010|ps=.|p=900}}</ref> On the waterfront, there are two Greek Revival houses on St. George's waterfront, at 404 and 272 Richmond Terrace. == Police and crime ==
[[File:120 Precinct Richmond Terrace jeh.jpg|thumb|NYPD 120th Precinct station house]]
St. George and the North Shore are patrolled by the 120th Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department|NYPD]], located at 78 Richmond Terrace.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/120th-precinct.page|title=NYPD – 120th Precinct|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref> The 120th Precinct ranked 12th safest out of 69 patrol areas for per-capita crime in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/staten-island/st-george/|title=St. George – DNAinfo.com Crime and Safety Report|website=www.dnainfo.com|access-date=October 6, 2016|archive-date=April 15, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170415062736/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/staten-island/st-george|url-status=dead}}</ref> {{As of|2018}}, with a non-fatal assault rate of 94 per 100,000 people, St. George and the North Shore's rate of [[violent crime]]s per capita is more than that of the city as a whole. The incarceration rate of 719 per 100,000 people is higher than that of the city as a whole.<ref name="CHP2018">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/data/2018chp-si1.pdf|title=St. George and Stapleton (Including Grymes Hill, Mariner's Harbor, Port Richmond, Stapleton, St. George, West Brighton and Westerleigh)|date=2018|website=nyc.gov|publisher=NYC Health|access-date=March 2, 2019}}</ref>{{Rp|8}}

The 120th Precinct has a lower crime rate than in the 1990s, with crimes across all categories having decreased by 83.3% between 1990 and 2022. The precinct reported seven murders, 14 rapes, 118 robberies, 384 felony assaults, 124 burglaries, 338 grand larcenies, and 136 grand larcenies auto in 2022.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-120pct.pdf|title=120th Precinct CompStat Report|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=July 22, 2018}}</ref>

== Health ==
{{As of|2018}}, [[preterm birth]]s and births to teenage mothers are more common in St. George and the North Shore than in other places citywide. In St. George and the North Shore, there were 96 preterm births per 1,000 live births (compared to 87 per 1,000 citywide), and 22.6 births to teenage mothers per 1,000 live births (compared to 19.3 per 1,000 citywide).<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|11}} St. George and the North Shore have a relatively average population of residents who are [[Health insurance coverage in the United States|uninsured]]. In 2018, this population of uninsured residents was estimated to be 12%, the same as the citywide rate of 12%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|14}}

The concentration of [[particulates|fine particulate matter]], the deadliest type of [[air pollution|air pollutant]], in St. George and the North Shore is {{convert|0.0071|mg/m3|oz/ft3}}, less than the city average.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|9}} Sixteen percent of St. George and the North Shore residents are [[Smoking|smokers]], which is higher than the city average of 14% of residents being smokers.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} In St. George and the North Shore, 24% of residents are [[Obesity|obese]], 9% are [[Diabetes mellitus|diabetic]], and 26% have [[hypertension|high blood pressure]]—compared to the citywide averages of 24%, 11%, and 28% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|16}} In addition, 21% of children are obese, compared to the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|12}}

Eighty-seven percent of residents eat some fruits and vegetables every day, which is the same as the city's average of 87%. In 2018, 77% of residents described their health as "good", "very good", or "excellent", equal to the city's average of 78%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} For every supermarket in St. George and the North Shore, there are 28 [[convenience store|bodegas]].<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|10}}

The nearest major hospital is [[Richmond University Medical Center]] in West New Brighton.<ref>{{cite web | title=Best 30 Hospitals in Staten Island, NY with Reviews | website=Yellow Pages | date=December 1, 2009 | url=https://www.yellowpages.com/staten-island-ny/hospitals | access-date=March 19, 2019}}</ref>

== Education ==
[[File:NYPL Saint George Branch, Staten Island.jpg|thumb|New York Public Library, St. George Library Ctr]]
St. George and the North Shore generally have a lower rate of college-educated residents than the rest of the city {{as of|2018|lc=y}}. While 37% of residents age 25 and older have a college education or higher, 15% have less than a high school education and 48% are high school graduates or have some college education. By contrast, 39% of Staten Island residents and 43% of city residents have a college education or higher.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} The percentage of St. George and the North Shore students excelling in math rose from 49% in 2000 to 65% in 2011, though reading achievement declined from 55% to 51% during the same time period.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://furmancenter.org/files/sotc/SI_01_11.pdf|title=St. George / Stapleton – SI 01|date=2011|publisher=[[Furman Center for Real Estate and Urban Policy]]|access-date=October 5, 2016}}</ref>

St. George and the North Shore's rate of elementary school student absenteeism is slightly higher than the rest of New York City. In St. George and the North Shore, 25% of elementary school students missed twenty or more days per [[school year]], more than the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="nyc.gov 2016">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/tcny/community-health-assessment-plan.pdf|title=2016-2018 Community Health Assessment and Community Health Improvement Plan: Take Care New York 2020|date=2016|website=[[government of New York City|nyc.gov]]|publisher=[[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene]]|access-date=September 8, 2017}}</ref>{{Rp|24 (PDF p. 55)}}<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} Additionally, 73% of high school students in St. George and the North Shore graduate on time, about the same as the citywide average of 75%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}}

=== Library ===
The [[New York Public Library]] (NYPL)'s [[St. George Library Center]] is located at 5 Central Avenue, across from Staten Island's Borough Hall and County Courthouse. The St. George Library Center, Staten Island's main library, was built in 1906–1907; it was designed by Carrère and Hastings in the [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] Revival style.<ref name="EDC p. 5" /><ref name="AIA5 p. 898" /><ref name="The New York Public Library" /> The branch contains three stories, including a basement. The first floor contains the main reading room, while the second floor contains a children's collection, and the lower level contains a collection for young adults.<ref name="The New York Public Library">{{cite web | title=About the St. George Library Center | website=The New York Public Library | url=https://www.nypl.org/about/locations/st-george-library-center | access-date=March 14, 2019}}</ref>

St. George Terminal is served by nearly all Staten Island bus routes, except for the {{NYC bus link|S53|S54|S55|S56|S57|S59|S79 SBS|S89|prose=y}}, as well as the [[Staten Island Railway]] and the [[Staten Island Ferry]].<ref>{{Cite NYC bus map|S}}</ref> Additionally, St. George is also served by the [[NYC Ferry]]'s St. George route.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scribd.com/doc/254611698/Proposed-Routes-for-NYC-s-Expanded-Ferry-Service|title=Proposed Routes for NYC's Expanded Ferry Service|author=DNAinfoNewYork|website=Scribd|access-date=September 22, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amny.com/transit/nyc-ferry-routes-1.25782023|title=NYC Ferry is adding 2 new routes|date=January 10, 2019|website=am New York|access-date=January 11, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://ny.curbed.com/2019/1/10/18177078/nyc-ferry-transportation-staten-island-coney-island|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190112044224/https://ny.curbed.com/2019/1/10/18177078/nyc-ferry-transportation-staten-island-coney-island|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 12, 2019|title=NYC Ferry will launch service to Staten Island, Coney Island|last=Plitt|first=Amy|date=January 10, 2019|website=Curbed NY|access-date=January 11, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ferry.nyc/nycferry-2020-2021-service-route-expansion/|title=2020-2021 Expansion|website=New York City Ferry Service|access-date=January 11, 2019}}</ref>

== Telephone exchange ==
In 1924, the "Saint George" [[telephone exchange]] was established in the new North Staten Island building of [[New York Telephone]], one of the island's five such exchanges. It became "SAint George 7" <!-- Please don't "correct" the standard double capital notation for phone prefixes --> when New York City's service underwent a major upgrade six years later. This three-digit prefix, now identified by numbers as "727", is the last of the five pre-upgrade exchanges still in service.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nydailynews.com/connection-telephone-exchanges-gave-line-neighborhood-article-1.752800|title=Connection To The Past Once, Telephone Exchanges Gave You A Line On The Neighborhood|last=Diehl|first=Lorraine B.|date=April 27, 1997|website=nydailynews.com|access-date=November 20, 2019}}</ref> Due to the abbreviation of "Saint" in the name of "Saint George", some historic telephone books such as those of the NYPD mistakenly gave the exchange as "ST. George 7", which directed the caller to an exchange in Manhattan.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/04/06/archives/other-city-police-heed-calls-fast-survey-of-11-areas-in-us-shows.html|title=OTHER CITY POLICE HEED CALLS FAST; Survey of 11 Areas in U.S. Shows They Overcome Problems Found Here; CENTRAL PHONING USED; One Emergency Number to Dial Contrasts With 5 for New York's Boroughs|date=April 6, 1964|work=The New York Times|access-date=November 20, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>
